title: The Collector of Prints
credit: H. O. Havemeyer Collection, Bequest of Mrs. H. O. Havemeyer, 1929
caption_tea: The identity of the print collector Degas painted has never been confirmed, but the room around him is filled with things Degas himself loved to collect -- Japanese fabric, Redouté-style botanical lithographs, and a Tang dynasty figurine -- turning the sitter's obsession into a mirror of the artist's own.

title: Self-Portrait
caption_tea: Van Dyck likely painted this self-portrait around age twenty-one, during a stay at the English court in the winter of 1620-21, not long before he left for Italy to spend six formative years studying Titian's color and brushwork.

title: Saints Peter, Martha, Mary Magdalen, and Leonard
caption_tea: Painted for a church in Correggio's own hometown, the altarpiece pairs each saint with an attribute -- Peter's keys, Martha's tamed dragon, Mary Magdalen's ointment jar, Leonard's prisoner's fetters -- while giving all four the same haunting, inward absorption that made Correggio one of the Renaissance's most original painters.

title: The Temptation
caption_tea: True to Pietro Longhi's gift for wry Venetian genre scenes, the picture shows a gentleman at breakfast being announced the arrival of a courtesan and her procuress -- a second cup and saucer already set out gives away that he was expecting her.

title: Aegina Visited by Jupiter
credit: Gift of Harry N. Abrams and Purchase, 1970
caption_tea: Greuze never exhibited or titled this canvas in his lifetime, so its subject -- likely Aegina being courted by Jupiter disguised as an eagle -- was pieced together only later by scholars; it may be the ambitious nude Greuze once told the critic Diderot he wanted to paint without offending propriety.

title: Christ Healing the Blind
credit: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Charles Wrightsman, 1978
caption_tea: Painted in Venice around 1570, before El Greco ever set foot in Spain, the work shows him absorbing Venetian Renaissance lessons in perspective and gesture; he left the upper-left corner unfinished, offering a rare glimpse of his loose underlying sketch.

title: Madonna and Child
caption_tea: Bellini pulls back the curtain behind the Madonna to reveal a landscape shifting from barren hills to a lush, verdant town -- a quiet visual metaphor for resurrection and renewal behind the sacred scene.

title: Madonna and Child
caption_tea: This is one of only two paintings that can be confidently attributed to Berlinghiero, the leading painter of Lucca in his day; it follows the Byzantine Hodegetria type -- "She Who Shows the Way" -- that reached Italy after icons flowed west following the fall of Constantinople in 1204.

title: The Vision of Saint John
caption_tea: Painted in the last years of El Greco's life for a Toledo hospital church, this apocalyptic vision of martyred souls receiving robes of salvation was cut down from a larger altarpiece and later studied intently by Picasso while he was developing Les Demoiselles d'Avignon.

title: Virgin and Child with Saint Catherine of Alexandria
caption_tea: Saint Catherine, shown here with the pearls and martyr's palm of a princess, was venerated by young women for her legendary "mystical marriage" to Christ; the painting's warmth and rhythm reflect how deeply Van Dyck had absorbed Titian and Veronese during his years working in Italy.

title: Sebastián Martínez y Pérez
caption_tea: The sitter's inscription reads "Don Sebastián Martínez by his friend Goya, 1792" -- Goya painted it while recovering in Martínez's Cádiz household during the illness that soon left him permanently deaf, and he posed his host, a noted collector, contemplating a print.

title: Virgin and Child with the Young Saint John the Baptist and Angels
credit: Gift of Adelaide Milton de Groot, 1966
caption_tea: Boucher painted this intimate devotional scene in 1765, the same year he was named director of the French Royal Academy, tucking Eucharistic grapes and the young Baptist's lamb into what could almost pass for a pastoral idyll.

title: A Woodland Road with Travelers
caption_tea: Jan Brueghel the Elder was born shortly before the death of his famous father, Pieter Bruegel the Elder, and pushed Northern landscape painting further with atmospheric perspective -- note how the travelers and terrain grow paler and hazier the deeper the road recedes into the woods.

title: The Three Ages of Humans
caption_tea: Dosso Dossi painted this allegory of youth, love, and old age not long after becoming court artist to Duke Alfonso I d'Este of Ferrara, hiding two boys peering from behind a bush, a pair of lovers, and two elderly men within one idyllic, sun-dappled landscape.

title: Cardinal Fernando Niño de Guevara
credit: H. O. Havemeyer Collection, Bequest of Mrs. H. O. Havemeyer, 1929
caption_tea: Niño de Guevara became Spain's inquisitor general in 1599, and El Greco likely painted him the following year on official Inquisition business in Toledo; painter Mary Cassatt spotted the portrait and urged the Havemeyers to buy it, a purchase that took collector Louisine Havemeyer four difficult years to pull off.

title: The Entombment
caption_tea: Painted just before Moretto's own death for a lay confraternity's chapel in his hometown of Brescia, the altarpiece was meant as a meditation on mortality, pairing the mourners' somber faces with dawn light breaking across the sky -- a contrast between grief and the promise of life to come.

title: The Triumph of Henry IV
caption_tea: This oil sketch was one small step toward a planned forty-eight-canvas cycle glorifying Marie de' Medici's husband, Henry IV, to hang alongside the queen's own completed cycle at the Palais du Luxembourg -- a companion series left mostly unfinished after Marie was banished from France in 1631.

title: Clothing the Naked
credit: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Charles Wrightsman, 1984
caption_tea: This scene illustrates one of the traditional Seven Acts of Mercy, reduced by Sweerts to a tense standoff between a richly dressed man and a wary, unclothed figure; painted in Amsterdam around the same years Sweerts practiced fasting and other devotional discipline, its deep shadow and individualized faces recall Rembrandt's work of the same period.

title: Don Gaspar de Guzmán, Count-Duke of Olivares
caption_tea: Mazo trained in Diego Velázquez's studio and married his teacher's daughter in 1633, later inheriting Velázquez's court position; this equestrian portrait shows Gaspar de Guzmán, Count-Duke of Olivares, who served as Philip IV of Spain's powerful prime minister from 1621 to 1643.

title: Cottage Children (The Wood Gatherers)
caption_tea: Wealthy eighteenth-century collectors loved these sentimental "fancy pictures" of poor children; a visitor to Gainsborough's studio called the trio "charming little objects," and the pensive boy with his bundle of kindling is thought to be modeled on Jack Hill, a local boy the artist's own daughter considered adopting.

title: Josefa de Castilla Portugal y van Asbrock de Garcini
caption_tea: Painted as a pendant to Goya's portrait of her husband, Colonel Ignacio Garcini, this informal portrait of Josefa -- loose-haired, in a simple dress, holding a small fan -- stayed in the Garcini family for over a century before both paintings were sold in 1910 and eventually bequeathed to the Met.

title: Ignacio Garcini y Queralt, Brigadier of Engineers
caption_tea: Goya painted this portrait of the military engineer Ignacio Garcini as a pendant to his wife Josefa's likeness in the same year, 1804; the pair stayed together in the Garcini family for over a century before entering the Met's collection through the same bequest.

title: Wolf and Fox Hunt
caption_tea: This monumental canvas, painted with workshop assistants in 1616, was the first in a new genre Rubens essentially invented: giant hunting scenes that offered wealthy patrons a cheaper, faster alternative to tapestries -- though Rubens insisted the wolves themselves were painted entirely by his own hand.

title: The Visit
credit: H. O. Havemeyer Collection, Bequest of Mrs. H. O. Havemeyer, 1929
caption_tea: De Hooch set this scene in a voorhuis, the best-lit street-facing room of a Dutch row house, at a time when he was in close visual dialogue with his contemporary Johannes Vermeer; the plate of oysters and the canopied bed are period clues suggesting the room may be a brothel rather than a respectable home.

title: A Forest at Dawn with a Deer Hunt
credit: Purchase, The Annenberg Foundation and other gifts, 1990
caption_tea: Rubens painted this in the final years of his life after acquiring the manor of Het Steen in 1635, when hunting -- an aristocratic privilege -- suited his new identity as lord of his own estate; the scene's dawn light, filtered through Titian-inspired color and brushwork, casts the hunt as a contest between light and darkness itself.

title: Charles Claude de Flahaut, Comte d'Angiviller
credit: Gift of Edith C. Blum Executors, 1966
caption_tea: At the time Greuze painted him in 1763, the young Comte d'Angiviller was already overseeing the household of the future Louis XVI; he would go on to become general director of the Bâtiments du Roi, a post that made him the closest thing eighteenth-century France had to a culture minister deciding artists' careers.

title: The Silver Tureen
caption_tea: Chardin builds this still life around a quiet tension between the living and the dead: a cat crouches at the left eyeing a game rabbit and a dead bird laid out beside fruit and a gleaming silver tureen, each surface -- fur, feather, citrus peel, polished metal -- rendered convincingly without ever hiding the roughness of the paint itself.

title: Herman Doomer
credit: H. O. Havemeyer Collection, Bequest of Mrs. H. O. Havemeyer, 1929
caption_tea: Herman Doomer was Amsterdam's leading cabinetmaker, prized for pioneering ebony furniture inlaid with mother-of-pearl; Rembrandt painted this portrait of him in 1640, the same year Doomer's son Lambert was apprenticing in Rembrandt's own studio, and made a companion portrait of Doomer's wife now in the Hermitage.

title: Madame Charles Maurice de Talleyrand Périgord
caption_tea: Talleyrand's marriage to this sitter in 1802 was so scandalous that Napoleon himself demanded the pair wed; the paisley shawl she wears is a modish accessory but also a quiet nod to her birth near Pondicherry in French colonial India, and by the time Gérard painted her the couple had already separated.

title: Jewish Woman of Algiers
medium: Onyx-marble, bronze, gilt bronze, enamel, amethyst
credit: European Sculpture and Decorative Arts Fund, 2006
caption_tea: Cordier discovered deposits of Algerian onyx-marble on a trip to Algeria in 1856 and began carving polychrome busts from it; a Marseilles gaming club commissioned this bust as one of a rare matched pair of women, part of Cordier's larger project of pioneering ethnographic sculpture to argue, in his words, for "the universality of beauty."

title: Bib for a Statuette
medium: Polychromed lead, glass, silver, silk lace
caption_tea: This tiny bib was made for one of the elaborately costumed figures in the Met's Neapolitan Baroque crèche, a set of more than two hundred eighteenth-century Nativity figures donated by collector Loretta Hines Howard in 1964 -- Naples's noble families took genuine pride in dressing such statuettes in real silk, lace, and jewels, down to accessories this small.

title: Watch
medium: Agate, onyx cameo, enameled gold, gemstones
caption_tea: The man carved into this watch's onyx cameo was long thought to be a sixteenth-century Fugger banker, but surviving Fugger portraits don't match him -- he more likely belongs to the early seventeenth-century "Dürer revival" fashion among Augsburg's goldsmiths and watchmakers.

title: Woman from the French Colonies
credit: European Sculpture and Decorative Arts Fund, 2006
caption_tea: Cordier titled this bust "Câpresse des Colonies," a period term for a woman of mixed Black and biracial parentage from France's Caribbean colonies; he made it in the years following the 1848 abolition of slavery in the French empire, an event that shaped his broader project of sculpting ethnographic subjects to argue for what he called "the universality of beauty."

title: The Little Fourteen-Year-Old Dancer
credit: H. O. Havemeyer Collection, Bequest of Mrs. H. O. Havemeyer, 1929
caption_tea: Degas modeled this on Marie van Goethem, a young Belgian student at the Paris Opera Ballet school, and it was the only sculpture he ever exhibited in his lifetime -- the original 1881 wax figure wore a real cotton bodice, linen ballet slippers, and a human-hair wig, and the Met has restrung and replaced this bronze cast's fabric tutu at least three times since acquiring it.

title: Alexander Danilovich Menshikov
bio: Swiss, Austrian, or German, active Russia ca. 1703–4
caption_tea: This bust's sitter went unidentified for years until researchers Wolfram Koeppe and Marina Nudel pieced together clues in the armor and wig to name him as Alexander Menshikov, Peter the Great's closest confidant; it is carved from red pine stained to imitate boxwood and assembled with metal clips, a technique typical of German and Austrian workshops rather than Russian ones -- fitting, since Menshikov is known to have employed foreign craftsmen.

title: Rothschild Lamp
medium: Bronze, on a later wood base
credit: European Sculpture and Decorative Arts Fund, 2009
caption_tea: Riccio -- Italian for "curly-haired," the nickname he was known by -- was the leading bronze sculptor of Renaissance Padua, and this is considered the finest of only six surviving lamps of this complexity by his hand; it spent the nineteenth century in the collection of Baron James Mayer de Rothschild and his heirs before reaching the Met in 2009.

title: The Thinker
caption_tea: Originally titled The Poet, this figure was conceived to sit above the lintel of Rodin's monumental bronze doorway The Gates of Hell, brooding over the damned souls of Dante's Inferno below him; that vast doorway, commissioned for a museum that was never built, was never even cast in bronze during Rodin's own lifetime.

title: Sprite
credit: Purchase, Mrs. Samuel Reed Gift and other funds, 1983
caption_tea: Records show that in 1436 a fountain was installed in the courtyard of Cosimo de' Medici's Florentine house, topped by a gilded spiritello -- almost certainly this very figure -- whose sculptor, clearly familiar with Donatello's bronze angels for the Siena Baptistery, blended traits of Mercury, god of commerce beloved by the Medici, with those of the wind-god Zephyr.

title: Spinario (Boy Pulling a Thorn from His Foot)
caption_tea: At just seven and a half inches tall, this bronze miniaturizes one of ancient Rome's most celebrated statues, the life-size Spinario now in Rome's Capitoline Museums; Antico likely made it for a member of the Gonzaga family, capturing in tiny scale the boy's total concentration on pulling a thorn from his own foot.

title: The Farnese Table
caption_tea: Designed for Cardinal Alessandro Farnese and weighing some thirty thousand pounds, this pietre-dure tabletop was so prized that whenever the cardinal traveled, servants covered it in leather and locked it inside a padlocked wooden case.

title: Waistcoat
caption_tea: Anna Maria Garthwaite was one of the era's leading silk pattern-drawers working out of Spitalfields in London, turning out as many as eighty floral designs a year for master weavers to sell to fashionable clients; surviving records even name the weaver who wove this exact pattern, Peter Lekeux, and give its sale date of October 23, 1747.

title: Print after Orazio Samacchini
caption_tea: This anonymous etching mirrors, in reverse, a painting by the Bolognese Mannerist Orazio Samacchini now in the Pinacoteca Nazionale in Bologna -- a reminder that reproductive prints like this one were how most people in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries ever got to "see" a famous altarpiece they could never visit in person.

title: Sketches from Nature
caption_tea: Rowlandson was best known for biting satirical caricatures of Georgian society, so this gentler hand-colored plate from his late-career "Sketches from Nature" series shows a different side of him -- a genuine, observational delight in the English countryside rather than social ridicule.

title: Aux Bains de Mer
caption_tea: This lithograph belongs to Daumier's "Aux Bains de Mer" series, published in the satirical Parisian newspaper Le Charivari in September 1859, poking fun at fashionable city-dwellers awkwardly adjusting to seaside vacation manners and the new craze for sea bathing.

title: Mascarade à la Grecque; Suite des Vases
caption_tea: Petitot invented these fantastical costumes -- a shepherdess, a priestess, a monk, a sutler in outlandish architectural dress -- as a gentle joke aimed at the "Greek taste" craze that swept French fashion and design in the 1750s.

title: A Sibyl Reading a Book Facing Left
artist: After Raphael; print attributed to Ugo da Carpi
caption_tea: Ugo da Carpi is credited as the first Italian printmaker to master the chiaroscuro woodcut -- building an image from several wood blocks inked in different tones to mimic a wash drawing -- and he was proud enough of the invention to win an exclusive printing privilege from the Venetian Senate in 1516, followed by a papal privilege in 1518, the year this sheet after Raphael's design was made.

title: An Apostle
credit: Harris Brisbane Dick Fund, by exchange, 1970
caption_tea: Almost nothing is recorded about Angiolo Falconetto beyond a small handful of surviving etchings, including companion prints of Saint James Major and Saint Matthew -- suggesting this apostle was originally one figure in a now-scattered series, a rare trace of a printmaker who otherwise left barely a mark on history.

title: A Sibyl Reading a Book Facing Left
artist: After Raphael; print attributed to Ugo da Carpi
caption_tea: This is a later pull of the same chiaroscuro woodcut design Ugo da Carpi based on Raphael's Cumaean Sibyl, printed from multiple carved wood blocks inked in graded tones -- a technique da Carpi considered his own invention and defended with an exclusive Venetian printing privilege.

title: Pensive Bodhisattva
credit: Purchase, Walter and Leonore Annenberg and The Annenberg Foundation Gift, 2003
caption_tea: The pensive bodhisattva -- shown deep in thought before choosing to delay enlightenment to help others -- was one of the most important Buddhist icons in Korea's Baekje and Silla kingdoms; the orb-and-crescent motif topping this figure's crown points to Central Asian influence carried along trade routes into the Korean peninsula.

title: Octagonal Cup with Ring Handle
caption_tea: This cup's fluted, ring-handled shape follows imported Sogdian silverware from Central Asia, brought to China along the Silk Road; Sogdian merchants also helped popularize grape wine in Tang China, and new drinks called for new vessels like this one, adapted by Chinese silversmiths from foreign models.

title: Man with a Shovel
caption_tea: Figures like this laborer were made as mingqi, spirit goods molded in earthenware and placed in Tang dynasty tombs so that the deceased would have servants and workers on hand to attend to them in the afterlife.

title: Panel in the Shape of a Sarcophagus Door
caption_tea: Carved to imitate the paneled door of a stone sarcophagus, this limestone slab reflects a Tang dynasty burial custom of housing the dead in miniature architectural forms decorated with auspicious motifs like the phoenix, meant to guard and honor the deceased in the afterlife.

title: The Art of Conversation
medium: Woodblock print; ink and color on paper
credit: Gift of Estate of Samuel Isham, 1914
caption_tea: Suzuki Harunobu was the innovator behind nishiki-e, the full-color woodblock printing technique he helped pioneer around 1765, using multiple hand-carved blocks to layer color onto paper in a process that transformed Japanese printmaking almost overnight.

title: Diptych of Kali / Tara, Wrathful Protectors
credit: Gift of Mark Baron and Elise Boisanté, 2018
caption_tea: When chromolithography arrived in Calcutta in the 1860s, print workshops like this one quickly began mass-producing images of Kali for household worship, capitalizing on her deep local significance as the presiding deity of the city's Kalighat Temple.

title: Goddess Kamalatmika
credit: Purchase, The Kipper Family Foundation Gift, 2021
caption_tea: Kamalatmika, "she of the lotus," is a tantric form of the goddess Lakshmi and one of the ten Mahavidyas, or wisdom goddesses; here she is enthroned on a lotus rising from a mountain lake while four elephants pour water from golden pitchers over her, an image of abundance meant for popular devotional display rather than temple ritual.

title: Encyclopedia of Western Art (Kōmō Zatsuwa)
caption_tea: Published during Japan's era of Rangaku, or "Dutch Learning," this five-volume illustrated book gathered Morishima Chūryō's notes on European geography, customs, and curiosities gleaned from conversations with the Dutch traders confined to the man-made island of Dejima -- Japan's only officially sanctioned window onto the West during its centuries of seclusion.

title: Medallion with Return from a Spring Outing
credit: Purchase, Friends of Asian Art Gifts, 1993
caption_tea: At just over an inch tall, this densely carved ivory shows a scholar-gentleman returning home from a night of wine and poetry, his attendants hurrying to open the gate ahead of him -- it is one of only a small number of Chinese ivory carvings that can be confidently dated to the Ming period.

title: Linga with Face of Shiva (Ekamukhalinga)
credit: Purchase, Friends of Asian Art Gifts, 1989
caption_tea: This is an ekamukhalinga, a form showing Shiva's face emerging from his aniconic linga symbol, a type of image that rose to prominence in North India starting in the fifth century; the crescent moon in his piled, double-looped hair is one of the god's signature attributes, alongside the third eye marking his supreme wisdom.

title: Buddha Flanked by Avalokiteshvara-Padmapani and Vajrapani
credit: Purchase, Friends of Asian Art Gifts, 2008
caption_tea: This molded-clay shrine group is among the most complete surviving examples from Tibet's early Buddhist period, pairing the Buddha with Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion, and Vajrapani, embodiment of enlightened energy -- a trio whose joint veneration played a central role in Buddhism's introduction to Tibet.

title: Egypt, from the Du Camp album
caption_tea: Maxime Du Camp made these views while traveling up the Nile with his friend, the future novelist Gustave Flaubert, hauling a wooden calotype camera, a tripod, and jugs of chemicals across Egypt between 1849 and 1851; the resulting album, published in 1852, is considered the first French book ever illustrated with photographs.

title: Egypt, from the Du Camp album
caption_tea: This salted paper print comes from the roughly 125 images Du Camp selected for his 1852 album Égypte, Nubie, Palestine et Syrie, printed by Blanquart-Évrard in Lille -- one of the first travel photography books ever produced and an instant sensation when it appeared.

title: Egypt, from the Du Camp album
caption_tea: Du Camp and his traveling companion, the novelist-to-be Gustave Flaubert, sailed up the Nile as far as the second cataract before drifting back downriver at a leisurely pace, stopping along the banks to photograph ancient sites -- a journey that produced one of the earliest substantial photographic surveys of Egypt's monuments.

title: Egypt, from the Du Camp album
caption_tea: Working with a bulky wooden calotype camera and glass jugs of chemicals lugged across the desert, Du Camp produced negatives that were printed onto salted paper by the Lille firm of Blanquart-Évrard for his landmark 1852 album -- one of photography's first great travel books.

title: Egypt, from the Du Camp album
caption_tea: Published in 1852, Du Camp's album of some 125 Egyptian views was the first French book ever illustrated with photographs, printed using the salted-paper process that Louis Désiré Blanquart-Évrard had pioneered only a few years earlier.

title: Egypt, from the Du Camp album
caption_tea: Du Camp traveled through Egypt in the company of his close friend Gustave Flaubert, soon to become one of France's greatest novelists, documenting ancient monuments with a calotype camera on a journey that turned into one of photography's earliest travel albums.

title: Egypt, from the Du Camp album
caption_tea: This print is one of roughly 125 images Du Camp brought back from his 1849-51 expedition up the Nile, later published as Égypte, Nubie, Palestine et Syrie -- a book credited with essentially inventing the genre of the photographically illustrated travel account.

title: Union Cavalry Soldier with Pistol in Holster
medium: Albumen silver print from glass negative
credit: Purchase, Vital Projects Fund Inc. Gift, 2019
caption_tea: This unidentified cavalryman from Indiana was among the millions of ordinary Civil War soldiers who sat for small studio portraits like this one before heading off to the front -- cheap, quick albumen prints that let families keep a likeness of a loved one who might never come home.

title: Young Woman with Beckers Tabletop Stereoscope
medium: Albumen silver print from glass negative
caption_tea: The tabletop stereoscope in this portrait was designed in 1857 by the New York daguerreotypist Alexander Beckers; its rosewood cabinet stored a stack of stereo slides that a viewer could flip through in succession by turning a knob, making it an early forerunner of the home slideshow.

title: Marie Antoinette in a Park
medium: Black chalk, stumped, and white chalk; framing lines in black chalk
caption_tea: This is Vigée Le Brun's only known drawing of Marie Antoinette, even though she painted the queen more than two dozen times in oil. The sheet went unattributed for over a century and was only identified as her work in 1982, just before it was sold from the Christian Humann collection.

title: Hermann von Wedigh III (died 1560)
caption_tea: A slip of paper tucked into the sitter's book bears a Latin motto from the Roman playwright Terence, "truth breeds hatred" - likely the young merchant's personal credo - while the signet ring on his hand displays the coat of arms of the Wedigh family of Cologne.

title: Antoine Perrenot de Granvelle
medium: Engraving, with touches of gray wash
credit: The Elisha Whittelsey Collection, The Elisha Whittelsey Fund, 2022
caption_tea: Granvelle, who rose from bishop to cardinal and from royal secretary to independent statesman within a decade, deliberately cultivated his image as a learned patron of the arts through engraved portraits like this one, which circulated his likeness across Europe.

title: Portrait of a Woman with a Man at a Casement
credit: Marquand Collection, Gift of Henry G. Marquand, 1889
caption_tea: Painted around 1440, this is the earliest known double portrait in Italian art and the first to set its sitters in a domestic interior opening onto a landscape. The woman's embroidered cuff spells out "lealta" (loyalty) in pearls, hinting that she and the man at the window, possibly Lorenzo di Ranieri Scolari and Angiola di Bernardo Sapiti, were newly betrothed.

cast.name: Lorenzo di Ranieri Scolari
cast.tidbit: If the traditional identification is correct, Lorenzo was a Florentine from a family whose coat of arms appears to be held in the man's clasped hands -- the main visual evidence behind the identification in the first place.

cast.name: Angiola di Bernardo Sapiti
cast.role_in_scene: Seated in profile, in French-inspired dress
cast.tidbit: If the traditional identification is correct, Angiola married Lorenzo di Ranieri Scolari around 1436 -- her embroidered cuff spells out "lealta" (loyalty) in pearls, read as a reference to that betrothal.

cast_context.text: A Met curator first proposed this identification a century ago based on a coat of arms in the painting, and it remains unproven -- a 1987 counterproposal argued the arms belong to a different family entirely, so the couple's names, and even whether the picture marks a marriage or a birth, stay genuinely open questions.

title: Portrait of a Woman, Possibly a Nun of San Secondo; (verso) Scene in Grisaille
medium: Oil on wood; (verso: oil and gold on wood)
caption_tea: Barely bigger than a playing card, this miniature and its pendant portrait of a Venetian nobleman form the core of Jacometto's tiny surviving body of work; paintings this small and finely detailed were likely meant to be held in the hand rather than hung on a wall.

title: Portrait of a Young Man
credit: H. O. Havemeyer Collection, Bequest of Mrs. H. O. Havemeyer, 1929
caption_tea: The sitter, never identified, holds a book of poetry and likely belonged to Bronzino's own literary circle in Florence, which included the poet Laura Battiferri; the carved grotesque heads on the furniture and the mask-like folds of his breeches hide the kind of witty visual puns Bronzino also composed in verse.

title: Philip IV (1605–1665), King of Spain
artist: Velázquez (Diego Rodríguez de Silva y Velázquez)
caption_tea: This is Velázquez's earliest fully documented portrait of the young king, painted soon after his appointment as court painter in Madrid; a courtier paid for this autograph replica of a now-lost first version on December 4, 1624. Centuries of overpaint had so obscured the canvas that the Museum downgraded its attribution to "workshop of Velázquez" for decades, until cleaning revealed the master's own hand.

title: Antoine Laurent Lavoisier (1743–1794) and Marie Anne Lavoisier (Marie Anne Pierrette Paulze, 1758–1836)
credit: Purchase, Mr. and Mrs. Charles Wrightsman Gift, in honor of Everett Fahy, 1977
caption_tea: Marie Anne Lavoisier, shown leaning on her husband's shoulder, was a trained scientific illustrator who etched the plates for his chemistry treatises. Conservators at the Met discovered in 2019 that David had first painted the couple as far flashier aristocrats, complete with a plumed hat and gilded furniture, before reworking the canvas into the sober tribute to science seen today.

cast.name: Antoine-Laurent Lavoisier
cast.role_in_scene: Seated at his desk with chemistry apparatus
cast.tidbit: Widely called the father of modern chemistry for naming oxygen and hydrogen and dismantling the old phlogiston theory of combustion, Lavoisier was guillotined in 1794 during the Terror -- the same revolutionary suspicion of the wealthy that had already forced this portrait out of public exhibition.

cast.name: Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier
cast.role_in_scene: Standing at her husband's side, resting a hand on his shoulder
cast.tidbit: She trained under David, the very painter of this portrait, to draw and engrave the illustrations for her husband's chemistry publications, and taught herself English specifically to translate papers by Priestley and Cavendish that he couldn't read himself.

cast_context.text: Married in 1771 in an arranged match between two well-off families, Antoine and Marie-Anne built an unusually equal scientific partnership -- she translated the English-language chemistry he couldn't read himself and illustrated his publications, work substantial enough that historians now credit her as a collaborator rather than merely a supportive spouse.

title: James-Jacques-Joseph Tissot (1836–1902)
caption_tea: Degas and Tissot were close friends from their student days in Florence, and here Degas surrounds him with signs of his artistic ambitions, including a copy of a Northern Renaissance portrait and a Japanese-style painting on the studio wall behind him.

title: Self-Portrait
caption_tea: Rosa paints himself inscribing a human skull with a Greek phrase meaning "Behold, whither, at length," a memento mori theme reinforced by his mourning cypress wreath and a book by the Stoic philosopher Seneca. An inscription reveals he gave the painting to his close friend, the Pisan scholar Giovanni Battista Ricciardi.

title: Self-Portrait with Two Pupils, Marie Gabrielle Capet (1761–1818) and Marie Marguerite Carraux de Rosemond (1765–1788)
caption_tea: Exhibited at the Salon of 1785, this life-size canvas doubled as a quiet political statement: after Labille-Guiard and Vigée Le Brun were admitted to the Royal Academy in 1783, membership for women artists was capped at just four, and this image of a confident teacher and her students argued for expanding that number.

cast.name: Adélaïde Labille-Guiard
cast.role_in_scene: Seated at her easel in the blue dress, teaching
cast.tidbit: One of only four women admitted to the French Royal Academy in the 18th century, Labille-Guiard was also the first woman granted her own studio at the Louvre for training pupils -- a privilege this very painting was exhibited to help justify.

cast.name: Marie-Gabrielle Capet
cast.role_in_scene: Seated beside her teacher, in the brown dress
cast.tidbit: Capet moved in with Labille-Guiard as both pupil and companion, later specializing in portrait miniatures -- some historians think deliberately, to avoid competing directly with her teacher's reputation in oils -- and stayed with her until Labille-Guiard's death.

cast.name: Marie-Marguerite Carreaux de Rosemond
cast.role_in_scene: Standing in the background, in white
cast.tidbit: One of nine young women singled out for praise at the 1783 Exposition de la Jeunesse, Carreaux de Rosemond married the engraver Charles Clement Balvay in 1788 and died later that same year from complications of childbirth, in the Louvre galleries where she had trained.

cast_context.text: Painted the same era women's membership in the Royal Academy was capped at four, Labille-Guiard's self-portrait with two of her own students reads as an argument for lifting that cap -- proof, staged for the Salon audience, that a woman could run a serious studio and train the next generation.

title: L'Arlésienne: Madame Joseph-Michel Ginoux (Marie Julien, 1848–1911)
caption_tea: Marie Ginoux ran the Café de la Gare in Arles, where Van Gogh lodged in 1888. When Gauguin visited that November, the two artists painted her in the same sitting, with Gauguin sketching her in charcoal in under an hour while Van Gogh completed a full canvas.

title: Madame Cézanne (Hortense Fiquet, 1850–1922) in the Conservatory
caption_tea: Hortense Fiquet, a former artist's model, met Cézanne around 1869 and sat for at least twenty-nine known portraits over more than two decades, more than any other model in his career. This canvas remains visibly unfinished, letting viewers see how he built up her face before completing the surrounding conservatory.

title: Don Andrés de Andrade y la Cal
credit: Bequest of Collis P. Huntington, by exchange, 1927
caption_tea: Murillo adopted this grand full-length format, complete with an imposing dog, after studying portraits by Titian, Velázquez, and Van Dyck during a trip to Madrid. Almost nothing else is known today about the sitter beyond his name and coat of arms, rendered in trompe l'oeil on the stone pilaster beside him.

title: "Jahangir and his Father, Akbar", Folio from the Shah Jahan Album
medium: Ink, opaque watercolor, and gold on paper
credit: Purchase, Rogers Fund and The Kevorkian Foundation Gift, 1955
caption_tea: This folio comes from the Shah Jahan Album, an imperial Mughal scrapbook of paintings and calligraphy begun under Emperor Jahangir and later expanded by his son, Shah Jahan. Here the artist Balachand shows Jahangir raising his hands in a gesture of respect toward his father and predecessor, Akbar, who holds a hunting falcon.

cast.name: Akbar
cast.role_in_scene: Standing at right, holding a hunting falcon
cast.tidbit: Akbar expanded the Mughal Empire across most of the Indian subcontinent during his nearly 50-year reign and was known for a religious tolerance unusual for his era, hosting regular debates between Muslim, Hindu, Christian, and Zoroastrian scholars at his court.

cast.name: Jahangir
cast.role_in_scene: Standing at left, raising his hands in a gesture of respect toward his father
cast.tidbit: Jahangir actually rebelled against Akbar in 1599, impatient to take the throne while his father was away on campaign -- the revolt failed, but Akbar forgave him and confirmed him as heir before dying in 1605, and Jahangir went on to rule for 22 years, especially remembered for his patronage of painting.

cast_context.text: Despite the gesture of filial respect shown here, father and son had a genuinely contentious relationship -- Jahangir's 1599 revolt against Akbar nearly cost him the succession entirely, making this album folio's harmonious framing as much a statement of legitimacy as a record of affection.

title: The Last Toilet of Charlotte Corday
caption_tea: Charlotte Corday was executed by guillotine in 1793 for assassinating the radical revolutionary leader Jean-Paul Marat. This engraving, made after a Royal Academy painting by E. M. Ward, imagines her final hours in prison as a grim parody of a lady's dressing ritual, with a jailer cutting her hair for the blade in place of a hairdresser readying her for a ball.

title: Tobatsu Bishamonten
medium: Zelkova wood with traces of color
credit: Mary Griggs Burke Collection, Gift of the Mary and Jackson Burke Foundation, 2015
caption_tea: This fierce guardian king stands on the shoulders of the earth deity Jiten and two dwarf demons instead of the usual rock, marking him as Tobatsu, an independent form of Bishamonten who normally appears grouped with three other Guardian Kings of the four directions. He grips a miniature stupa containing the Buddha's relics in one hand, while his missing right hand originally held a weapon to subdue the enemies of Buddhist law.

title: "Abiding nowhere, the awakened mind arises"
credit: Mary and Cheney Cowles Collection, Gift of Mary and Cheney Cowles, 2018
caption_tea: The eight brushed characters transcribe a verse from the Diamond Sutra, rendered in a dynamic cursive script meant to convey that spiritual awakening comes from transcending the material world. Musō Soseki was among the most influential monks in early Japanese Zen, serving as spiritual advisor to both the reigning emperor and the shogun Ashikaga Takauji after relocating from Kamakura to Kyoto in 1333.

title: Statuette of a hippo goddess, probably Taweret
caption_tea: Part hippopotamus, part crocodile, and part lion, Taweret's fearsome hybrid form was meant to frighten away the demons that threatened women in childbirth. This statuette's fine craftsmanship and near-perfect condition suggest it was made for a temple's "birth house," where the goddess was closely linked with Isis.

title: "The Concourse of the Birds", Folio 11r from a Mantiq al-Tayr (Language of the Birds)
medium: Ink, opaque watercolor, gold, and silver on paper
caption_tea: In this scene from a twelfth-century Sufi mystical poem, the birds of the world gather in an idyllic landscape to seek the simurgh, a mythical bird symbolizing divine unity, before setting off on pilgrimage under a hoopoe's guidance. The manuscript that contains this folio is one of the most celebrated works of Persian book painting, begun in Timurid Herat and finished decades later at the Safavid court in Isfahan.

title: Ia Orana Maria (Hail Mary)
caption_tea: Painted within months of Gauguin's arrival in Tahiti, this is his first attempt to reimagine the Christian Madonna and Child through a Polynesian lens, casting a Tahitian mother and infant as Mary and Jesus beneath a golden halo and an attendant angel. The title is an everyday Tahitian greeting, so the painting's name translates roughly as "Hail Mary."

title: The Penitence of Saint Jerome
tags: Landscapes, Saint Jerome, Saint John the Baptist
caption_tea: Patinir folds three separate religious episodes - Christ's baptism, Jerome's penitence in the wilderness, and the temptation of Saint Anthony - into one continuous, panoramic landscape that shifts from green foreground to hazy blue horizon. That atmospheric perspective became his signature contribution to European painting, so admired that contemporaries praised him chiefly as a landscape specialist rather than a painter of religious figures.

title: Processional Cross
credit: Purchase, Elaine Rosenberg Gift and funds from various donors, 1998
caption_tea: Ethiopian priests fixed crosses like this one onto a wooden staff so they could be carried aloft during outdoor processions and liturgical services. Ethiopian crosses made before the seventeenth century survive only rarely, since many older examples were destroyed during sixteenth-century military campaigns that swept through the highlands.

title: The Fieschi Morgan Staurotheke
medium: Gilded silver, gold, enamel worked in cloisonné, and niello
caption_tea: Small enough to cup in one hand, this container once held a sliver of wood believed to come from the True Cross, one of Christendom's most sacred relics, and was likely made for private devotion rather than public display. Its lid depicts the crucified Christ flanked by the Virgin Mary and Saint John, surrounded by saints rendered in vivid cloisonné enamel.

title: Saint Bridget of Sweden Receiving the Rule of Her Order
caption_tea: This relief depicts a mystic vision that Saint Bridget recorded in her own writings, the Revelationes, in which Christ himself presents her with the rule for the religious order she founded in Sweden in 1346. Carved for an altar predella in Perugia that was dismantled just decades later, it portrays a subject rarely attempted in fifteenth-century sculpture.

title: Night-Shining White
caption_tea: This ink portrait shows a fiery cavalry horse owned by the Tang emperor Xuanzong, its flaring nostrils and dancing hooves capturing the spirited character prized in the imperial stables. More than a thousand years of collectors' seals and inscriptions crowd the mounting, tracing the scroll's passage through generations of connoisseurs.

title: Old Trees, Level Distance
medium: Handscroll; ink and color on silk
credit: Gift of John M. Crawford Jr., in honor of Douglas Dillon, 1981
caption_tea: Guo Xi was the leading landscape painter of the Northern Song court, and this handscroll is thought to be a late work made for a retiring official, its bare autumn trees and deepening mist lending the scene a wistful, valedictory mood. The composition follows his signature 'level-distance' formula, pairing tall foreground trees with a wide, misty river valley.

title: Fragrant Snow at Broken Bridge
credit: Ex coll.: C. C. Wang Family, Purchase, Gift of J. Pierpont Morgan, by exchange, 1973
caption_tea: Wang Mian was a peasant-born scholar who abandoned the imperial examinations and instead earned his living selling ink paintings of plum blossoms, one of the 'Four Gentlemen' flowers prized for symbolizing resilience through winter's hardship. Broken Bridge, near West Lake in Hangzhou, was already famous as a plum-viewing spot when he painted this scene.

title: Wangchuan Villa
medium: Handscroll; ink and color on paper
credit: Ex coll.: C. C. Wang Family, Purchase, Douglas Dillon Gift, 1977
caption_tea: Wang Yuanqi based this handscroll on a stone rubbing of the country retreat built by the Tang poet-painter Wang Wei, reimagining a garden that had vanished centuries earlier through both landscape and poetry. In a colophon he added afterward, the artist expressed satisfaction at having captured Wang Wei's ideal of 'painting in poetry and poetry in painting.'

title: Plum blossoms
medium: Album of twelve leaves; ink on paper
credit: Edward Elliott Family Collection, Gift of Douglas Dillon, 1986
caption_tea: Jin Nong, one of the so-called Eight Eccentrics of Yangzhou, took up plum-blossom painting only in his late sixties, reportedly completing this album during a six-week stay at a friend's home in 1757. His branches range from exuberant, blossom-laden sprays to single, spare twigs, each paired with his own poetic inscriptions.

title: Landscapes
medium: Album of eight paintings; ink and color on paper
credit: Gift of Florence and Herbert Irving Collection, in memory of Douglas Dillon, 2003
caption_tea: Xiao Yuncong remained loyal to the fallen Ming dynasty and refused to serve the conquering Qing, retreating instead into poetry and painting, including this album of river landscapes rendered in his characteristically dry, angular brushwork. He is remembered today as a founding figure of the Anhui school of landscape painting.

title: Bamboo in Snow
medium: Pair of hanging scrolls; ink on silk
credit: The Harry G. C. Packard Collection of Asian Art, Gift of Harry G. C. Packard, and Purchase, Fletcher, Rogers, Harris Brisbane Dick, and Louis V. Bell Funds, Joseph Pulitzer Bequest, and The Annenberg Fund Inc. Gift, 1975
caption_tea: Dapeng Zhengkun was a Chinese Buddhist monk who emigrated to Japan in 1722 and eventually became abbot of the Ōbaku Zen temple Manpuku-ji, where he was known by his Japanese name, Taihō Shōkon. Alongside his religious duties he built a reputation as a bamboo painter, developing a distinctive style of thick, curving stalks and diagonally crisscrossing leaves.

title: Carp and Waterweeds
credit: Mary Griggs Burke Collection, Gift of the Mary and Jackson Burke Foundation, 2015
caption_tea: Little is recorded of Yōgetsu beyond his life as a monk-painter working in the mountains near Nara, where he is thought to have followed the style of the master Sesshū Tōyō. A poem inscribed above his painting likens the carp to the mount of a Daoist immortal, linking the fish to ideas of transcendence.

title: White Poppies on Gold Ground
medium: Six-panel folding screen; color on paper
credit: H. O. Havemeyer Collection, Gift of Horace Havemeyer, 1949
caption_tea: The screen's flat, brilliantly colored poppies against a field of gold epitomize the decorative style later named 'Rinpa,' a term derived from the final syllable of Kōrin's own name. Kōrin signed the work 'Hokkyō Kōrin,' using an honorary rank the imperial court had granted him in recognition of his artistic standing.

title: Herbaceous Peony
medium: Folding fan mounted as an album leaf; ink and color on gold paper
credit: Gift of Robert Hatfield Ellsworth, in memory of La Ferne Hatfield Ellsworth, 1986
caption_tea: Painted on a folding fan in ink and color on gold paper, this peony blends literati restraint with more popular tastes: many scholar-painters considered gold grounds vulgar, but Hu Yuan used one anyway to set off a flower long associated with wealth and seductive beauty.

title: The Horse Fair
caption_tea: To study the horse trade firsthand, Bonheur spent a year and a half sketching at Paris's Boulevard de l'Hôpital horse market dressed in men's clothing, which let her move unbothered through a business dominated by men. Cornelius Vanderbilt purchased the finished canvas, over eight feet high and sixteen feet long, in 1887 and donated it to the Museum immediately.

title: A River in a Meadow
caption_tea: Rousseau was a founding figure of the Barbizon School, whose members left Paris for the countryside to paint directly from nature rather than compose idealized scenes in the studio. This tranquil view, with a lone figure receding into the distance, reflects the group's quiet devotion to the French landscape.

title: The Forest in Winter at Sunset
credit: Gift of P. A. B. Widener, 1911
caption_tea: Rousseau worked on this monumental view of the Fontainebleau forest on and off for roughly twenty years, trying to recapture a sunset he had witnessed there in December 1845, and it remained unfinished at his death despite friends urging him to complete it. Two small, stooped figures at its center are nearly swallowed by the tangle of bare, wintry trees.

title: Cows Crossing a Ford
credit: Gift of Mrs. Leon L. Watters, in memory of Leon Laizer Watters, 1967
caption_tea: Dupré painted this scene on the spot in the Limousin region of central France, and its low horizon and broadly brushed sky reveal the impact of a trip he made to England in 1834, where he studied the landscapes of John Constable. It was shown to acclaim at the Paris gallery Susse Frères the following summer.

title: Lake Fucino and the Abruzzi Mountains
medium: Oil on paper, laid down on canvas
credit: The Whitney Collection, Gift of Wheelock Whitney III, and Purchase, Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Charles S. McVeigh, by exchange, 2003
caption_tea: Bidauld painted this oil sketch outdoors at Avezzano, looking across a lake that was then the largest in the Abruzzi region of central Italy; engineers later drained it completely, so the view he recorded no longer exists. A colleague recalled that Bidauld painted or drew outdoors every day, in a different spot each time, treating each open-air study with the same care as a finished studio picture.

title: Irises
caption_tea: Van Gogh painted this bouquet in May 1890, just before checking himself out of the asylum at Saint-Rémy, pairing it with a canvas of roses in a deliberate exercise in complementary color contrast. He described his goal as a 'harmonious and soft' effect, though the violet blooms were originally set against a pink background that has since faded.

title: Wheat Field with Cypresses
caption_tea: Painted directly outdoors during Van Gogh's stay at the asylum in Saint-Rémy, this canvas was one he later singled out as among his best summer landscapes, and he went on to make two further studio versions of the same composition. He also sent his brother Theo reed-pen drawings of the scene to describe its effect.

title: Catania and Mount Etna
caption_tea: Better known today for his limericks and nonsense verse, Edward Lear was also a serious landscape painter who trekked to the summit of Mount Etna in June 1847 with his friend John Proby, inscribing this oil sketch with the exact date of the climb.

title: George Sand's Garden at Nohant
caption_tea: Delacroix painted this rare pure landscape as a gift for his close friend, the novelist George Sand, during one of his summer visits to her country home at Nohant in the early 1840s. It remained in Sand's possession for the rest of her life before passing to her son.

title: "Page of Calligraphy Illuminated with Animals and Plants in a Field of Flowers", Folio from the Shah Jahan Album
medium: Ink, opaque watercolor, and gold on paper
credit: Purchase, Rogers Fund and The Kevorkian Foundation Gift, 1955
caption_tea: This folio comes from the Shah Jahan Album, an imperial Mughal compilation of paintings and calligraphy begun under Emperor Jahangir and expanded under his son, for which the painter Nanha illuminated a page of calligraphy by the renowned scribe Mir 'Ali Haravi with a field of deer, flowers, and foliage.

title: Female Monkey Holding Its Baby
caption_tea: Monkeys were not native to Egypt but were imported as exotic pets, and this pose of a mother monkey cradling her young first appears on cosmetic jars as early as the Old Kingdom. Carved in amethyst, a stone favored for miniature animal figures in this era, the image carried associations of fertility and rebirth.

title: Stirrup-spout bottle with feline and snake
credit: Harris Brisbane Dick and Fletcher Funds, 1967
caption_tea: The jaguar and boa constrictor on this bottle were likely linked to visions produced by the San Pedro cactus, a hallucinogen used in Cupisnique ritual; participants who ingested it were thought to transform into one of several powerful animals. Its stirrup-shaped spout, named for its resemblance to a saddle stirrup, remained the signature vessel form of Peru's north coast for some 2,500 years.

title: Jug in the form of a recumbent bull
caption_tea: This bull-shaped jug, its curled tail forming the spout, was excavated from a buried cache at Chigha Sabz in the Luristan region of western Iran alongside inscribed cylinder seals dating to the 8th–6th centuries BCE. Animal-form vessels like this one were a hallmark of Iron Age pottery from the region.

title: Double-chambered bottle with monkeys
caption_tea: Topará potters of Peru's south coast, working around two thousand years ago, fused two hollow monkey-shaped vessels together with a flat bridge handle, burnishing the surfaces to a uniform shine. The monkeys' wide eyes and half-open mouths, one hand touching an ear and the other its mouth, give them an air of startled surprise.

title: The New Testament, The Book of Common Prayer
medium: Silk, bullion, silver, and silver-gilt thread on canvas and satin
caption_tea: Embroidered bindings like this one were a fashionable domestic needlework practice in England under Charles I: gentlewomen covered devotional books in canvas worked with silk, metallic thread, and spangles, often padding figures into raised stumpwork relief.

title: Upholstery panels for a settee
credit: The Lesley and Emma Sheafer Collection, Bequest of Emma A. Sheafer, 1973
caption_tea: These painted silk panels once covered a suite of Rococo settees carved for the "Green Trellis Chamber," a garden room at Seehof Palace near Bamberg; the seat backs were carved to resemble garden trelliswork entwined with flowers, onto which the painted Chinese export silk was mounted.

title: Panel for a skirt or petticoat
credit: Purchase, Friends of European Sculpture and Decorative Arts Gifts, 2011
caption_tea: This crewelwork panel belongs to a wave of chinoiserie embroidery that swept English needlework around 1700: inspired by imported Asian silks, porcelain, and lacquer, embroiderers invented fantastical hybrid landscapes of pagodas, exotic birds, and Chinese-costumed figures they had never actually seen.

title: Quilt, Presentation pattern
caption_tea: Simon is thought to have sold pre-cut, basted appliqué quilt blocks as kits to Baltimore needlewomen between 1846 and 1854. This quilt is nearly identical to a dated 1849 example made as a wedding gift, and its own inscription patch was cut away and replaced with plain fabric before quilting, erasing the name of whomever it once honored.

title: Valentine with lace paper and faux pearls
medium: Cameo-embossed lace paper, chromolithographed die-cuts, faux pearls, blue satin, white satin ribbon, gold paper stars, graphite, ink, watercolor
caption_tea: Howland built her elaborate valentines on a base of imported English lace paper made by the firm Mansell, then layered on chromolithographed die-cuts, silk, and paper flowers by hand. This example still carries a penciled inscription tucked inside one of its lift-up flaps: "Elizabeth Rowe Bogert from Augustus Bogert."

title: Torah crown (keter)
caption_tea: Engraved with priestly garments, the Tablets of the Law, and a miniature Temple, the crown carries a later Hebrew inscription recording that it was given as a "crown of glory, and diadem of beauty" by the philanthropist Gabriel Trieste to his Jewish congregation in Padua in the mid-19th century, long after its creation in Venice.

title: Mirror with Split-Leaf Palmette Design Inlaid with Gold
caption_tea: Believed to have been made in an Ottoman court workshop in Bursa or Istanbul, this steel mirror's gold-inlaid spiral vine scrolls and chevron-patterned handle closely echo a more lavish jade-handled mirror in Istanbul's Topkapi Palace, suggesting both came from the same royal atelier.

title: Longcase clock
medium: Case: rosewood, coniferous wood veneered with mahogany and inlaid with bands of holly, stained holly and bone, and brass; Dial: painted enamel on copper with brass hour hands; Movement: brass and steel
caption_tea: The case's surface is built entirely from contrasting inlaid woods and bone -- bands of holly, stained holly, and brass -- a decorative technique called stringing that English cabinetmakers used to trace fine geometric patterns across furniture without carving.

title: One of a Pair of Vases with Dragon Handles
medium: Cloisonné enamel with gilt bronze and champlevé
caption_tea: This vase combines two related enameling techniques: cloisonné, where colored enamel is set within soldered wire compartments, and champlevé, where the metal itself is carved out to form recessed cells -- a technical pairing that became a hallmark of Qing-dynasty decorative metalwork.

title: Two-handled bowl from Burghley House, Lincolnshire
date: Chinese porcelain 1573– ca. 1585, British mounts ca. 1585
caption_tea: This Wanli-period blue-and-white bowl was fitted with English silver mounts almost as soon as it reached London, likely for Elizabeth I's chief minister William Cecil, Lord Burghley. The gilt-silver mounts borrow ornament from Antwerp design books, and the bowl later passed through the collections of J. Pierpont Morgan before reaching the Met.

title: Enameled and Gilded Bottle
medium: Glass, greenish; blown, folded foot; enameled and gilded
caption_tea: Very few painted glass vessels of this scale survive intact. The frieze of mounted, mace-wielding warriors beneath a soaring phoenix likely depicts a mock-combat horsemanship exercise, with riders costumed as combatants from the rival Ilkhanid and Mamluk states.

title: Standing shelf (one of a pair)
medium: Lacquered and painted pine, mahogany and British walnut
caption_tea: Linnell's shelf imitates East Asian lacquer through japanning, a European technique of building up layers of varnish and paint to mimic Chinese and Japanese lacquerwork. It originally furnished Badminton House, seat of the Dukes of Beaufort, until it was sold at auction in 1921.

title: Potpourri jar
medium: Soft-paste porcelain decorated in underglaze blue
credit: Gift of R. Thornton Wilson, in memory of Florence Ellsworth Wilson, 1950
caption_tea: This jar is one of only a handful of surviving pieces of Rouen soft-paste porcelain, a short-lived 1690s experiment to imitate Chinese porcelain that never reached commercial production. No museum outside France owns another example, making the Met's jar the only one abroad.

title: Pierced Bowl Signed by Hasan al-Qashani
medium: Stonepaste; molded and pierced, monochrome decoration under transparent glaze
credit: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Lester Wolfe, 1968
caption_tea: A Kufic inscription on the bowl reads "Made by Hasan al-Qashani," his name linking him to Kashan, the central Iranian town that held a near-monopoly on the newly developed stonepaste ceramic body -- a fine white paste that let potters pierce and mold vessel walls into openwork patterns impossible in ordinary earthenware.

title: Tankard with Peony Scroll
medium: Porcelain painted with cobalt blue under transparent glaze (Jingdezhen ware)
credit: Gift of Stanley Herzman, in memory of Adele Herzman, 1991
caption_tea: Despite its charming dragon-shaped handle, this tankard's overall form isn't Chinese at all -- it copies Islamic metalwork drinking vessels, since Jingdezhen potters in the early 15th century were producing blue-and-white wares specifically for export to Middle Eastern markets.

title: Brush washer with lotus
medium: Stoneware with incised decoration under a celadon glaze (Longquan ware)
caption_tea: Longquan celadon was exported for more than five hundred years, turning up from Japan and Southeast Asia to the Islamic world and Europe. But a small, finely incised piece like this brush washer was made for a scholar's writing desk at home rather than for the export trade.

title: Bowl with coat of arms of the Horsmanden family
credit: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Rafi Y. Mottahedeh, 1975
caption_tea: Armorial services painted with a patron's heraldic crest became the signature luxury commission of the China trade in the 18th century; patrons sent engraved bookplates or wax seals to Canton so that painters an ocean away could copy their family's coat of arms precisely onto porcelain.

title: Apostle plate with inscription of Saint Phillip
credit: Gift of Luísa Vinhais and Jorge Welsh, in honor of Mr. and Mrs. Renato de Albuquerque, 2016
caption_tea: Inscribed "S. Philippus" on a painted scroll, this plate belonged to a series depicting each of the twelve apostles, a devotional subject Chinese export painters at Jingdezhen copied from European religious prints supplied by Catholic patrons in Portugal or its colonies.

title: Creamer with cover (part of a service)
credit: Helena Woolworth McCann Collection, Purchase, Winfield Foundation Gift, 1961
caption_tea: The Dutch East India Company commissioned the artist Cornelis Pronk to draw designs of women, birds, and landscapes that were shipped to China so Jingdezhen painters could copy them onto porcelain. Only a handful of complete Pronk-pattern services survive today, making pieces like this creamer rare.

title: Plate
medium: Soft-paste porcelain decorated in polychrome enamels
credit: Purchase, Gift of Mrs. George Whitney, Mrs. William C. Breed and funds from various donors, by exchange, 2014
caption_tea: The London Bow factory painted this plate's landscape and peony border by directly copying a Chinese export plate made some twenty years earlier during the Yongzheng period, down to its rose-pink palette -- an English porcelain works imitating a Chinese imitation of European taste.

title: Punch bowl
caption_tea: Large punch bowls like this were among the showiest pieces a China trade merchant could order, painted with a coat of arms surrounded by hunting scenes. Only one complete armorial service design from this era survives intact, made about 1740 for the English gentleman Leake Okeover.

title: Tureen with cover
credit: Helena Woolworth McCann Collection, Purchase, Winfield Foundation Gift, 1964
caption_tea: Grand covered tureens were the centerpiece of a fashionable dinner service, and this one's eagle-crested coat of arms would have been copied in Canton workshops from a wax seal, engraved bookplate, or heraldic drawing sent from Europe specifically for the commission.

title: Platter
caption_tea: This platter belonged to a dinner service ordered for Samuel and Judith Verplanck's house on Wall Street in New York. Its European-style floral border is so close to contemporary Meissen porcelain patterns that, without the family's unbroken ownership record, it might easily be mistaken for a service made for the German or Scandinavian market.

title: Sabine Houdon (1787–1836)
medium: White marble on gray marble socle
caption_tea: This is a portrait of the sculptor's own daughter, one of a series of busts Houdon made of his three daughters as they grew; when it was sold at the 1928 auction of Judge Elbert H. Gary's collection it fetched $245,000, the highest price then ever paid for a sculpture at auction, a record it held for more than four decades.

title: Emperor Antoninus Pius
medium: Bronze, partially oil-gilt, silver inlay, on serpentinite socle
caption_tea: Antico gave Antoninus Pius an unusually vivid, transitory expression, a departure from the calm self-possession he gave his other busts of emperors and mythological figures; he made it for the Gonzaga court in Mantua, where he worked as sculptor, medalist, and antiquities adviser.

title: The Composer André-Ernest-Modeste Grétry (1741–1813)
credit: Purchase, Josephine Bay Paul and C. Michael Paul Foundation Inc. Gift and Charles Ulrick and Josephine Bay Foundation Inc. Gift, 1969
caption_tea: Commissioned in 1804 and installed at the Paris Opéra-Comique in 1809, the bust remained on view there until 1887; carved into the column beneath the composer are the names of forty-one of the roughly sixty operas Grétry wrote for the Opéra-Comique and the Académie de Musique.

title: Vessel in form of horned quadruped
caption_tea: Horned-animal vessels like this one were a distinctive product of Iron Age workshops in western Iran, where potters folded ordinary jugs into animal forms and pierced a spout through the body or tail; the style flourished during Iron Age III, roughly the eighth through sixth centuries BCE, when the region's bronze and pottery workshops grew increasingly inventive with animal imagery.

title: Stela of the Steward Mentuwoser
caption_tea: Carved by order of King Senwosret I for his steward Mentuwoser, this stela was set up at Abydos, one of Egypt's holiest sites; its sixteen columns of text single out Mentuwoser's honesty and his care for the poor, virtues recorded here alongside his official titles as steward and overseer of the king's granaries and herds.

title: Yuny and His Wife Renenutet
caption_tea: Yuny, a chief royal scribe from Asyut who may also have served as a physician, sits beside his wife Renenutet, her arm draped affectionately around his shoulders while she holds a beaded counterweight called a menat; carved into the back of their shared chair, their son offers to them in one register while Renenutet in turn offers food and drink to her own parents in another, a small family tableau spanning three generations.

cast.name: Yuny
cast.tidbit: Yuny served as a chief royal scribe and physician under Seti I around 1290 BCE, following his own father Amenhotep, who held the same post of chief physician before him.

cast.name: Renenutet
cast.role_in_scene: Seated beside her husband, arm around his shoulders
cast.tidbit: Renenutet held the title Singer of Amun, a respected temple role reserved for women of standing, and is shown here holding a menat -- a beaded counterweight used as both jewelry and a ceremonial musical instrument tied to that office.

cast_context.text: Carved for their tomb chapel at Asyut, this pair statue follows a long Egyptian tradition of commemorating husband and wife together for eternity -- the back of their shared chair carries a small family tableau across three generations, showing their son making offerings to them, and Renenutet in turn offering to her own parents.

title: Head from a Figure with a Beaded Headdress
caption_tea: Reportedly found at Rayy in Iran, this nearly circular head follows a 'moon-faced' beauty ideal drawn from Central Asian models favored under the Seljuks; an unfinished patch left on the back suggests it once leaned against a wall or sat in an architectural niche, so it may be a fragment of a larger palace figure rather than a complete sculpture in its own right.

title: Bowl with cover (perfume burner)
caption_tea: Giuseppe de' Levi, a bronze founder probably of Jewish origin working in Verona, habitually signed his pieces -- this bowl carries a cast inscription on its underside reading, in translation, '1599, de Rossi and Giuseppe de Levi of Verona made this' -- and its decoration, though it likely held burning perfume, is entirely secular, made for a wealthy household's cabinet rather than any devotional use.

title: Head of a ruler
caption_tea: Probably representing Rimush, son and successor of Sargon of Akkad, this head is among the earliest known life-size sculptures made with hollow lost-wax casting, a technically demanding method mastered in Mesopotamia over four thousand years ago; centuries of exposure to moisture and salts have corroded its once-smooth surface to the rough green patina seen today.

title: Marble portrait of the emperor Augustus
caption_tea: After the Roman senate granted Octavian the title Augustus in 27 BCE, an official portrait type was devised to broadcast the new emperor's authority across the empire, and versions of it, like this one, were carved and distributed by the hundreds -- making this marble head one small piece of history's first empire-wide image campaign.

title: Marble head from a statue of Harmodios
date: 1st–2nd century CE (Roman copy of a Greek bronze of 477/6 BCE)
caption_tea: This head comes from a Roman copy of one of the most celebrated statues in ancient Greece: the bronze Tyrannicides, erected in the Athenian Agora in 477/6 BCE to honor Harmodios and Aristogeiton for assassinating a son of the tyrant Peisistratos, and for a century afterward the only statues of ordinary citizens permitted to stand in that civic space.

title: Marble seated harp player
caption_tea: One of only a handful of known Cycladic sculptures to depict a musician, this seated harpist was carved with his head tipped back as though absorbed in his own playing, and the harp's frame ends in the carved head of a waterbird; like most Cycladic marble figures it was probably once painted in bright pigment, of which only faint traces now survive.

title: Head of King Amenemhat III
credit: Gift of Dr. and Mrs. Thomas H. Foulds, 1924
caption_tea: Egyptian sculptors typically gave aging pharaohs an idealized, youthful face even late in long reigns, and this head, likely carved around Amenemhat III's thirty-year jubilee, follows that convention -- rounder and softer than portraits of his predecessor Senwosret III, yet with deep creases beside the nose that hint at the greater realism creeping into royal portraiture by the end of the twelfth dynasty.

title: Horn Player
credit: The Michael C. Rockefeller Memorial Collection, Gift of Nelson A. Rockefeller, 1972
caption_tea: British soldiers seized this figure from the royal palace in Benin City during the 1897 Punitive Expedition, after which it was coated in England with oil varnish and pigmented wax to make it look more 'ancient' by Victorian taste; Met conservators only began stripping away that colonial-era coating in 1980, work that revealed casting techniques fundamentally different from contemporary European bronze-making.

title: Leopard
credit: The Michael C. Rockefeller Memorial Collection, Gift of Nelson A. Rockefeller, 1972
caption_tea: The leopard, Benin's 'king of the bush,' was one of the Oba's core emblems, standing for his ferocity and singular authority; cast brass plaques from the same court show the Oba ritually sacrificing live leopards in an annual ceremony meant to renew his mystical power, making sculpted leopards like this one a recurring motif across Benin's brass and ivory arts.

title: Equestrian figure
bio: Lower Niger Bronze Industry, Nigeria (15th–19th century)
credit: The Michael C. Rockefeller Memorial Collection, Bequest of Nelson A. Rockefeller, 1979
caption_tea: This bronze horse and rider belongs to a body of work art historians group under the term 'Lower Niger Bronze Industry' -- copper-alloy sculpture found across the Niger Valley that shares stylistic traits with Benin and Ife casting but can't be traced directly to either court workshop, a reminder of how much West African bronze-casting history still resists tidy attribution.

title: Hip ornament with Portuguese head
bio: Edo peoples, Kingdom of Benin (16th–19th century)
credit: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Klaus G. Perls, 1991
caption_tea: Benin chiefs wore cast brass pendants like this one at the hip or chest during palace ceremonies to signal rank and loyalty to the Oba; this one depicts a Portuguese visitor in the same generalized, stylized facial conventions Benin artists used for their own rulers, since status here was conveyed through dress and ornament rather than individualized features.

title: Camel and Rider
credit: Gift of Florence and Herbert Irving, 2015
caption_tea: Figures like this camel and rider were made as 'spirit utensils,' or mingqi, buried in tombs to serve the deceased in the afterlife; camels became an increasingly common tomb subject in this period as trade along the Silk Road brought Central Asian caravans, and their foreign drivers, into the northern Chinese imagination.

title: A Maid Asleep
caption_tea: X-ray and infrared analysis have revealed that Vermeer originally painted a man standing in the doorway behind the sleeping maid, along with a small dog at her feet, then painted over both figures, leaving the scene quieter and more ambiguous than he first intended.

title: The Fortune-Teller
caption_tea: A well-dressed young man has his fortune read by an old Romani woman while her three companions quietly pick his pocket and cut the medal from around his neck, a moralizing tale of deception that was a favorite subject in French Baroque genre painting.

title: The Smokers
credit: The Friedsam Collection, Bequest of Michael Friedsam, 1931
caption_tea: Brouwer painted himself into this tavern scene as the man turning toward the viewer with a raised tankard and a plume of smoke, surrounded by portraits of fellow painters including Jan Cossiers and the still-life specialist Jan Davidsz. de Heem.

title: A Peasant Family
caption_tea: Scholars still argue over which of the three Le Nain brothers, who often worked together in the same Paris studio, actually painted this intimate scene of rural life, since Antoine, Louis, and Mathieu shared such similar techniques that even specialists struggle to tell their hands apart.

title: Merrymakers at Shrovetide
caption_tea: The painting shows two stock characters from Dutch Carnival theater, Hans Worst with a sausage dangling from his cap and Pekelharing wreathed in salted fish, flanking a young woman who was almost certainly played by a boy, since women were barred from performing in Shrovetide plays.

title: The Chess Players
credit: Maitland F. Griggs Collection, Bequest of Maitland F. Griggs, 1943
caption_tea: This panel and its companion piece once decorated the front of a wedding chest and illustrate scenes from a now-unidentified romantic novella; here the young woman appears poised to win a flirtatious, high-stakes game of chess.

title: The Card Players
caption_tea: Cézanne painted five versions of card-playing peasants in the early 1890s; the smallest, showing just two men, was sold privately to Qatar's royal family in 2011 for a reported 250 million dollars, at the time the highest price ever paid for a painting.

title: Market by the Seashore
caption_tea: Small fishing boats have been hauled up onto a beach much like the one at Zandvoort, near Haarlem, while fishermen unload their catch and townspeople gather on the sand to buy directly from the boats, a scene of the everyday coastal fish trade.

title: Boating
credit: H. O. Havemeyer Collection, Bequest of Mrs. H. O. Havemeyer, 1929
caption_tea: Manet cropped the sailboat so abruptly and tilted its deck so steeply that the whole composition flattens like a Japanese woodblock print, an effect he and his fellow Impressionists admired; the sailor is thought to have been modeled by the artist's brother-in-law.

title: Young Woman Knitting
credit: Bequest of Miss Adelaide Milton de Groot (1876-1967), 1967
caption_tea: Morisot likely painted this scene outdoors at Bougival, where she summered for several years, and may have enlisted her daughter's nanny as the model for this fashionably dressed young woman knitting among the roses.

title: A Woman Reading
credit: Gift of Louise Senff Cameron, in memory of her uncle, Charles H. Senff, 1928
caption_tea: Corot, celebrated mainly for his landscapes, rarely exhibited figure paintings; this quiet scene of a woman absorbed in a book was one of the very few he showed publicly, at the Salon of 1869, when the artist was seventy-two years old.

title: At the Milliner's
medium: Pastel on pale gray wove paper (industrial wrapping paper), laid down on silk bolting
credit: H. O. Havemeyer Collection, Bequest of Mrs. H. O. Havemeyer, 1929
caption_tea: This pastel was the first of Degas's millinery-shop scenes to be shown publicly, at an 1882 exhibition in London; he became fascinated with the Paris hat trade, closely studying how feathers, flowers, and straw were arranged and sold to fashionable customers.

title: Seated Man Smoking a Pipe
credit: The Elisha Whittelsey Collection, The Elisha Whittelsey Fund, 2018
caption_tea: This etching belongs to a self-styled 'Second Suite of Figures' in which the young Alsatian-born printmaker deliberately imitated the loose, bravura etching style of the seventeenth-century Italian painter Salvator Rosa to show off his own skill with the needle.

title: Street vendor
credit: Gift of R. Thornton Wilson, in memory of Florence Ellsworth Wilson, 1954
caption_tea: Carved fully in the round, this porcelain figure only gives up its subject from certain angles: walk around it and the basket on the man's back turns out to be full of mushrooms he is peddling door to door, a popular type produced by the Mennecy factory under the protection of the Duc de Villeroy.

title: Tomb Chapel of Raemkai
caption_tea: Carved roughly 4,400 years ago for the tomb of a court official named Raemkai, these limestone reliefs once lined an offering chapel with scenes of everyday labor, including men gutting fish, baking bread, herding cattle, and slaughtering an ox, meant to magically sustain the deceased forever.

title: Damascus Room
medium: Wood (poplar) with gesso relief, gold and tin leaf, glazes and paint; wood (cypress, poplar, and mulberry), mother-of-pearl, marble and other stones, stucco with glass, plaster ceramic tiles, iron, brass
credit: Gift of The Hagop Kevorkian Fund, 1970
caption_tea: This is a reception room from the home of a wealthy Damascus family; its walls are inscribed with forty stanzas of poetry praising the Prophet Muhammad and the household's virtues, worked into carved and gilded wood alongside mother-of-pearl and marble inlay.

title: A Woman with a Dog
caption_tea: Ceruti earned the nickname 'Il Pitocchetto,' or 'the little beggar,' for devoting much of his career to painting servants, peddlers, and the poor with the same dignity usually reserved for wealthy sitters; here a maid holds her employer's pampered lapdog, a quiet joke about the gap between their circumstances.

title: Six Jewel Rivers from Various Provinces
medium: Six woodblock prints; ink and color on paper
credit: Mary Griggs Burke Collection, Gift of the Mary and Jackson Burke Foundation, 2015
caption_tea: Each print in this series pairs a classical poem with a scene of women at one of Japan's celebrated 'Tama' rivers, washing or pounding cloth by moonlight, turning an old courtly poetic theme into everyday genre scenes of women's work.

title: Still Life with a Skull and a Writing Quill
caption_tea: Working in an almost monochrome palette of grays and browns, Claesz arranged a toppled glass, a gap-toothed skull, and a guttering oil lamp on a stone ledge that seems to extend into the viewer's own space, turning the still life into a blunt reminder of how quickly life passes.

title: Still Life
caption_tea: Flegel is regarded as the first German painter to specialize in still life; over roughly thirty years in Frankfurt he produced around 110 small, tightly composed paintings of set tables, food, and flowers, of which this quiet arrangement is a rare survivor.

title: Basket of Fruit
caption_tea: Cavarozzi's composition directly echoes Caravaggio's famous basket of fruit in Milan, down to a worm-eaten quince and insect-nibbled leaves rendered under the same raking light, showing how quickly Caravaggio's still-life innovations spread among Roman painters.

title: Still Life: Balsam Apple and Vegetables
caption_tea: Peale arranged an unusually vivid array of vegetables, including okra, two kinds of cabbage, squash, eggplant, tomatoes, and the spiky orange balsam apple, in colors brighter than his usual subdued palette, making this one of his most celebrated still lifes.

title: Still Life with Teapot and Fruit
credit: The Walter H. and Leonore Annenberg Collection, Gift of Walter H. and Leonore Annenberg, 1997, Bequest of Walter H. Annenberg, 2002
caption_tea: Gauguin modeled this composition on a Cézanne still life he owned and treasured, swapping in mangoes for apples and a Tahitian printed cloth for French wallpaper; a year after finishing this picture, deep in debt, he was forced to sell that prized Cézanne.

title: Esneh (Latopolis), Construction Ensablée - Architrave, Futs, et Chapiteaux
medium: Salted paper print from paper negative
