caption_tea: Teynard was a civil engineer, not a professional photographer, who traveled more than a thousand miles up the Nile in 1851-52 to update Napoleon's decades-old "Description de l'Égypte" survey. His 160 salted-paper prints formed the most complete photographic record of the Nile Valley made to that date, though fewer than a dozen complete sets of the finished portfolio survive today.

title: [The Great Wave, Sète]
medium: Albumen silver print from glass negative
caption_tea: 1850s photographic plates could not register both sea and sky in one exposure without one washing out, so Le Gray printed two different negatives, one for the water and one for the clouds, onto the same sheet of paper. The seam is faintly visible at the horizon, but the trick made this one of the first photographs to convincingly freeze a moving sea.

title: Black Cañon, From Camp 8, Looking Above
medium: Albumen silver print from glass negative
credit: Purchase, Joseph Pulitzer Bequest and The Horace W. Goldsmith Foundation Gift through Joyce and Robert Menschel, 1986
caption_tea: O'Sullivan, a veteran Civil War photographer, joined Lieutenant George Wheeler's 1871 survey of the Colorado River and was given his own boat to haul his glass-plate darkroom through the rapids. His images of Black Canyon are among the earliest photographs of a landscape later submerged by the reservoirs of the Hoover and Davis dams.

title: Caroline Nightingale
medium: Albumen silver print from glass negative
caption_tea: Most surviving Victorian albumen portraits of private sitters like this one came from small, anonymous local studios rather than famous names, since the vast majority of 1870s portrait photographers never signed their prints. Here the sitter's identity, preserved only by an inscription, has outlasted any record of who actually made the picture.

title: [The Harvey Album]
credit: Purchase, The Horace W. Goldsmith Foundation Gift, through Joyce and Robert Menschel, 1998
caption_tea: Emily Clare Harvey made this album as a wedding gift for her sister-in-law in 1868, hand-painting watercolor borders around each pasted-in photograph, hunting motifs around a brother's portrait, flowers symbolizing affection around a female relative's, turning mass-produced studio cartes de visite into a one-of-a-kind keepsake.

title: Bourges
medium: Salted paper print from paper negative
credit: Gilman Collection, Purchase, The Horace W. Goldsmith Foundation Gift, through Joyce and Robert Menschel, 2005
caption_tea: For more than a century, the photographer who signed his salted-paper prints "Em. Pec" was unidentified in any photographic society record. Only in 2002 did research finally confirm him as Pierre-Émile-Joseph Pécarrère, a lawyer who had learned photography from Gustave Le Gray and photographed Gothic architecture across France in the early 1850s.

title: Emancipated Slaves Brought from Louisiana by Colonel George H. Hanks
medium: Albumen silver print from glass negative
credit: Gilman Collection, Purchase, The Horace W. Goldsmith Foundation Gift, through Joyce and Robert Menschel, 2005
caption_tea: In December 1863 a Union colonel brought eight formerly enslaved children and adults from occupied New Orleans to be photographed in New York, and cartes de visite like this one were sold to raise money for freedpeople's schools. One version of the image, captioned "White and Black Slaves from New Orleans," was designed to unsettle viewers who assumed slavery was visibly marked by skin color.

title: [Mugshots of Suspected Anarchists from French Police Files]
medium: Albumen silver prints and gelatin silver prints
caption_tea: Alphonse Bertillon, a Paris police clerk, invented the modern mug shot, a standardized front-and-profile photograph paired with precise body measurements, and applied it on a mass scale to anarchist suspects rounded up after a wave of bombings in the early 1890s. His method, called Bertillonage, was adopted by police departments worldwide before fingerprinting eventually replaced it.

title: Learning is Wealth—Wilson, Charley, Rebecca, and Rosa, Slaves from New Orleans
medium: Albumen silver print from glass negative
credit: The Horace W. Goldsmith Foundation Fund, through Joyce and Robert Menschel, 2011
caption_tea: Charles Paxson's studio portrait of four formerly enslaved children was sold as a carte de visite captioned "Learning is Wealth," part of an 1863-64 fundraising campaign that used photographs of children posed with schoolbooks to solicit donations for freedpeople's education in Union-occupied Louisiana.

cast.name: Wilson Chinn
cast.role_in_scene: Seated at left with a book
cast.tidbit: Formerly enslaved on a Louisiana plantation, Wilson Chinn was one of the adults who toured the North with these children as part of an 1863-64 campaign, appearing in a separate, widely reproduced photograph that documented the branding iron and shackles used on enslaved people.

cast.name: Charles "Charley" Taylor
cast.tidbit: Despite a complexion light enough that Union sympathizers used his photograph to argue slavery could ensnare people who looked white, Charley had been sold twice -- first by his own father and enslaver, Alexander Wethers of Virginia, to a trader who sold him on to a New Orleans owner.

cast.name: Rebecca Huger
cast.tidbit: Rebecca had been enslaved as her own father's household attendant to a girl only slightly older than herself; contemporary accounts noted that in the few months since her emancipation she had already learned to read and write.

cast.name: Rosina "Rosa" Downs
cast.role_in_scene: Seated with a book, not quite 7 years old
cast.tidbit: The youngest of the four, Rosa was photographed and toured alongside the others specifically because -- like Rebecca and Charley -- her fair complexion was used to unsettle Northern audiences into recognizing enslaved children as no different from their own.

cast_context.text: Brought north from Union-occupied Louisiana by Colonel George H. Hanks in 1863-64, these four formerly enslaved children and several adults toured Northern cities and were photographed to raise funds for the first schools for freedpeople in the Department of the Gulf -- Harper's Weekly ran engravings of the photographs alongside their biographies to fuel the campaign.

title: Sergeant John Lincoln Clem, The Drummer Boy of Chickamauga
artist: Morse & Peaslee, Gallery of the Cumberland
medium: Albumen silver print from glass negative
caption_tea: John Lincoln Clem ran away to join the Union Army at age nine and, by twelve, had reportedly fired on a Confederate officer at the Battle of Chickamauga, earning him the nickname captured in this portrait's title. He was made a sergeant later that year, making him one of the youngest noncommissioned officers in U.S. Army history.

title: Frank, Frederick & Alice. "The Children of the Battle Field"
caption_tea: When Sergeant Amos Humiston was found dead at Gettysburg clutching an image of his three children, a Philadelphia doctor published the picture in newspapers nationwide until the family was identified months later. The Philadelphia firm Wenderoth, Taylor & Brown then mass-produced this carte de visite of Frank, Frederick, and Alice to help fund the soldiers' orphanage built in their father's memory.

cast.name: Franklin "Frank" Humiston
cast.role_in_scene: The eldest of the three children, age 8 when the photograph was taken
cast.tidbit: Frank Humiston lived until 1912, later going by "Dr. Franklin Goodwin Humiston" -- one of three siblings whose mother, Philinda, positively identified them from this widely circulated photograph months after their father's death at Gettysburg.

cast.name: Alice Humiston
cast.role_in_scene: The middle child, age 6 when the photograph was taken
cast.tidbit: Alice and her siblings lived at the Soldiers' Orphans' Home built in Gettysburg with funds raised by sales of this photograph, where in 1868 the Humiston children placed flowers on their own father's grave during a Decoration Day ceremony.

cast.name: Frederick Humiston
cast.role_in_scene: The youngest child, age 4 when the photograph was taken
cast.tidbit: Frederick was barely more than a toddler when his father, Sergeant Amos Humiston, was found dead at Gettysburg still holding this photograph of his three children -- too young himself to remember his father, whose identity depended entirely on the picture being recognized by someone who did.

cast_context.text: Sergeant Amos Humiston died at Gettysburg clutching this photograph of his children with no other identification on him; a Philadelphia doctor published it in newspapers nationwide asking "Whose father was he?" until their mother recognized them months later -- the resulting fame turned the photograph into a fundraising tool for the soldiers' orphanage built in Humiston's memory.

title: [The Wilderness Battlefield]
medium: Albumen silver print from glass negative
credit: Gilman Collection, Purchase, The Horace W. Goldsmith Foundation Gift, through Joyce and Robert Menschel, 2005
caption_tea: G. O. Brown photographed skulls and unburied bones still scattered across the Wilderness battlefield in Virginia when Union surgeons returned to the site in April 1866, nearly two years after the fighting. The negative was apparently solarized during processing, leaving the print's sky with an eerie, tonally reversed glow.

title: Manem, dit Monem de Bretauville.
medium: Gelatin silver print from glass negative
caption_tea: This portrait belongs to the same anthropometric identification files compiled by the Paris police in the late nineteenth century as Alphonse Bertillon's better-known anarchist mugshots. The sitter's real name, Manem, is recorded here alongside an alias, "dit Monem de Bretauville," a reminder that police photography of this era was built specifically to pierce false identities.

title: Véret. 0ctave-Jean. 19 ans, né à Paris XXe. Photographe. Anarchiste. 2/3/94.
medium: Albumen silver print from glass negative
caption_tea: Octave-Jean Véret, photographed here at nineteen after his arrest as a suspected anarchist in 1894, listed his own occupation on Bertillon's police record as "Photographe": the very booking-photo technique used to identify him was also his trade.

title: [Departure for the huntTomb of Khan of Khiva]
credit: Gift of Charles K. and Irma B. Wilkinson, 1977
caption_tea: Luigi Pesce, an Italian army officer stationed in Persia to train the Shah's infantry, taught himself photography and self-funded expeditions across the region. He became the first photographer to capture Persepolis and other ancient Persian sites, presenting his portfolio to Naser al-Din Shah in 1858.

title: [Edward Charles Barnes]
credit: The Albert Ten Eyck Gardner Collection, Gift of the Centennial Committee, 1970
caption_tea: John and Charles Watkins ran a Parliament Street studio in London that photographed Queen Victoria, the Prince of Wales, and the exiled French royal family, riding the 1860s craze for collecting celebrity and society portraits as pocket-sized cartes de visite to be traded and pasted into albums.

title: Elise Parent (opéra) 1863
medium: Albumen silver print from glass negative
credit: Gilman Collection, Gift of The Howard Gilman Foundation, 2005
caption_tea: André-Adolphe-Eugène Disdéri patented a four-lensed camera in 1854 that exposed eight small portraits on a single glass plate, slashing the cost of a photographic likeness and making the carte de visite, and portraits of performers like the opera singer Elise Parent, a mass-collectible craze across Europe.

title: [Photo Collage: Man Wearing Cross Body Satchel]
credit: Gift of Drew Knowlton and William L. Schaeffer, 2017
caption_tea: Working from a Montevideo studio in the 1870s, Juan Pedro Chabalgoity spliced photographic portrait heads cut from albumen prints onto lithographed bodies and backgrounds, an unusual collage technique that let sitters appear in costumes and settings no camera in his studio could actually stage.

title: [Studio Portrait: Two Males Wearing Hats and Ponchos, Brazil]
credit: The Horace W. Goldsmith Foundation Fund, through Joyce and Robert Menschel, 2017
caption_tea: Ponchos like the ones worn here were standard rural dress across nineteenth-century South America, and studio photographers throughout Brazil and the neighboring River Plate region built a trade photographing regional "types" in such clothing for sale to travelers and collectors, much as William Carrick did with Russian street vendors in the same decade.

title: [Studio Portrait: Man in Coat Carrying Baskets, St. Petersburg]
credit: The Horace W. Goldsmith Foundation Fund, through Joyce and Robert Menschel, 2017
caption_tea: William Carrick, a Scottish photographer raised near St. Petersburg, opened a studio there in 1859 and spent his free time photographing the city's mail carriers, mushroom sellers, and other working people who walked the Nevsky Prospect, producing a series called "Russian Types" aimed at the tourist trade.

title: [Occupational Portrait of Kuban Cossack in Military Dress]
medium: Albumen silver print with applied color
caption_tea: This hand-tinted portrait of a Kuban Cossack in dress uniform is part of William Carrick's decades-long project documenting the ordinary people and regional costumes of Russia, work that today stands as one of the few detailed photographic records of everyday Russian life before the 1870s.

title: Self-Portrait
caption_tea: Rembrandt painted this self-portrait in 1660, the year after he was declared bankrupt and forced to sell his house and most of his art collection; the loose, thickly built-up brushwork on his face contrasts with the barely indicated clothing, as if the sitter's inner resilience mattered more to him than his ruined fortune.

title: Self-Portrait
medium: Watercolor, graphite, and gouache on paper
caption_tea: This watercolor is one of dozens of unflinching self-portraits Schiele made between 1910 and 1918, and it once belonged to Scofield Thayer, an American poet and Freud patient in Vienna who assembled a major collection of Schiele's and Klimt's work while undergoing psychoanalysis in the early 1920s.

title: Self-portrait
credit: Purchase, Harris Brisbane Dick Fund, by exchange, Anonymous Gift, and Virginia Marvin Stoughton Bequest, 2006
caption_tea: Copley painted this tiny watercolor-on-ivory self-portrait, just over an inch tall, in 1769 as a wedding gift for his new wife Susanna Clarke, alongside a nearly identical pastel version now held at Winterthur Museum in Delaware.

title: Self-Portrait
medium: Brush and point of brush, carbon black ink
caption_tea: Goya made this brush-and-ink self-portrait not long after a severe illness in 1792–93 left him permanently deaf; the drawing's searching, inward gaze is often read as a record of the isolated interior world he inhabited after losing his hearing.

title: A Brazilian Landscape
credit: Purchase, Rogers Fund, special funds, James S. Deely Gift, and Gift of Edna H. Sachs and other gifts and bequests, by exchange, 1981
caption_tea: Post painted this scene six years after returning home to Haarlem from Dutch Brazil, where he'd served the colonial governor Johan Maurits; the cactus and iguana in the foreground are souvenirs of that decade abroad, grafted onto a landscape built from thoroughly European conventions of perspective.

title: Embroidered panel with Grotesque decoration
caption_tea: The mythological scenes embroidered into this silk panel — Europa, Actaeon, Semele and others — were copied from woodcut designs by the French illustrator Bernard Salomon; it's one of a set of three, the other two of which remain in the Musée Historique des Tissus in Lyon.

title: Fragments of a marble statue of the Diadoumenos (youth tying a fillet around his head)
date: ca. 69–96 CE (Roman copy of a Greek bronze of ca. 430 BCE)
caption_tea: This Roman marble copy reproduces a bronze original by Polykleitos, the 5th-century BCE Greek sculptor famous for codifying an ideal system of bodily proportion; only the head, arms, lower legs, and tree-trunk support are ancient — the torso was recreated using a plaster cast of a different Diadoumenos copy now in Athens.

title: Marble statue of a kouros (youth)
caption_tea: Carved to mark the grave of a young Athenian aristocrat, this kouros is among the earliest life-size marble figures made in Attica, and its rigid stance with the left leg stepping forward was borrowed directly from Egyptian sculpture conventions.

title: Sword
credit: The Collection of Giovanni P. Morosini, presented by his daughter Giulia, 1932

title: Portrait of a Man, Possibly a Self-Portrait
artist: Velázquez (Diego Rodríguez de Silva y Velázquez)
caption_tea: The title's "possibly a self-portrait" comes from comparing the sitter's features to Velázquez's own face in Las Meninas, painted nearly two decades later -- the same heavy-lidded eyes and thick mustache, aged by time but unmistakably similar.
caption_basic: Portrait of a Man, Possibly a Self-Portrait by Velázquez (Diego Rodríguez de Silva y Velázquez) (ca. 1635) -- Oil on canvas
twist_hook: Demoted in 1979. Reinstated in 2009 -- from under the grime.
twist_story: Jules Bache paid dealer Joseph Duveen $1.125 million for this as a genuine Velázquez in 1926, and bequeathed it to the Met in 1949. By 1979, decades of yellowed varnish had dulled its color and blurred its brushwork past confident attribution, and the Museum downgraded it to "workshop of Velázquez." In 2009, conservator Michael Gallagher's cleaning changed that: murky greenish tones resolved into gray, and fine, confident brushwork emerged that scholars recognized as the master's own hand. Art historian Jonathan Brown put it simply: "The picture has been under my nose all my life." It re-entered the collection as an authentic Velázquez, not a copy.
